title: Can Students Catch Attention? Introducing Attention Contagion tagion/
author: Andrew Watson
summary: Andrew Watson unpacks 'attention contagion' research led by Dr. Noah Forrin, in which a trained confederate student sat near a genuine participant while both watched a 50-minute video. When the confederate paid close attention, the real student focused more, got less drowsy, took more notes, and remembered more on a later quiz, even when the confederate sat diagonally behind the participant, out of sight, meaning the effect propagated through cues like note-taking sounds rather than visible behaviour alone. Watson argues this shifts the practical target of attention-management from individual students to classroom-wide norms: rather than only redirecting one distracted student, teachers can work to ensure nearly all students are visibly and audibly engaged. He flags appropriate caveats -- only two studies exist on the phenomenon, conducted in artificial lab settings -- while still treating the finding as a genuinely useful new lens.
points: Forrin's research found that a neighbouring student's attentiveness or inattentiveness spreads to nearby students even when the inattentive student sits out of the observer's direct line of sight, likely through auditory cues like note-taking sounds.
The attentive-confederate effect was measurable across multiple channels: focus, drowsiness, note-taking volume, and quiz performance a week later.

Watson's key reframe: rather than targeting 'that-student-right-there' individually, teachers can build attentiveness at the level of whole-classroom norms, since a distracted student may 'catch' the room's collective attentiveness.

He is explicit about the evidence's limits -- only two studies exist, conducted in an artificial lab context -- and frames 'attention contagion' as a useful way to think, not yet a settled research conclusion.
quotes: That is: if Student A pays attention, will that attentiveness cause Student B to pay more attention as well? Or, if Student A seems inattentive, what happens with Student B?
Well, when A paid attention, B reported focusing more, focused more, got less drowsy, and fidgeted less, took more notes, and remembered slightly more on a subsequent multiple-choice quiz.
Sure enough, Forrin's team found the same results. Student B caught Student A's inattention, even if s/he couldn't see it.
If attention contagion is a thing, I can help that-student-right-there pay attention by ensuring ALL students are paying attention.
I should point out that the concept of 'attention contagion' is quite new — and its newness means we don't have much research at all on the topic.
